title: Benji Off the Leash!
full_review:
With the dearth of family-friendly movies, it is a doggone shame that when good-guy filmmaker Joe Camp comes along, his well-intentioned labors result in a woofer of a movie like "Benji Off the Leash!" (Mulberry Square).

The floppy-eared hero first strayed onto the big screen in "Benji" (1974), quickly followed by "For the Love of Benji" (1977) and a decade later by "Benji the Hunted" (1987). In addition to feature films, Benji also starred in numerous specials and even had his own TV series.

In the new film, set in rural Mississippi, the eponymous mutt (the fourth mixed terrier to fill the leash) befriends a shaggy but spunky mongrel named -- appropriately enough -- Shaggy, and helps him rescue his ailing mother from a squalid backyard puppy mill run by greedy breeder Hatchett (Chris Kendrick). The doggie duo is aided in their canine capering by Hatchett's pet-loving stepson, Colby (Nick Whitaker), and hampered by two bumbling dogcatchers (Randall Newsome and Duane Stephens). The story, which is layered with such serious issues as domestic abuse, was allegedly inspired by the real-life search for a new dog to play the title role.

Full of homespun charm, "Benji Off the Leash!" is the kind of little-movie-that-could which you desperately want to root for, but one which makes you leave the theater shaking your head in disappointment.

Camp, Benji's creator -- whose Mulberry Square Productions specializes in family fare -- hopes the film will prove that not everyone in the entertainment industry subscribes to the prevalent lowest-common-denominator mentality. Referring to his new film a "true 'everybody' movie," he wanted to make a movie that didn't rely on violence and vulgarity as selling points.

While such heart-in-the-right-place goals are certainly to be applauded and supported, neither the film's uplifting message nor its adorably scruffy stars can hide its poorly structured script, flat dialogue and stale performances, including the tedious slapstick antics of Newsome and Stephens. Sounds harsh, but to throw the film a more laudatory bone would be a clear case of letting the sentimental tail wag the dog of objectivity.

Sadly, "Benji Off the Leash!" is nothing to bark about.

Due to some mildly crude expressions, implied spousal abuse and images of animal cruelty, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG -- parental guidance suggested.
